title: Simplify Path
directAnswer: Split the path on '/', then process each component with a stack. Ignore empty strings (from '//') and '.' (current directory). For '..' pop one directory off the stack if it's non-empty (you can't go above root). Push any real directory name. Finally, join the stack with '/' and prepend a leading '/'. The stack naturally models 'go up = undo the last directory'. O(n) time, O(n) space.

remember.pattern: Tokenize on '/', use a stack to resolve '.' and '..'
rules: Split on `'/'` and **skip empty tokens** — consecutive slashes `//` and a trailing slash both produce `''`.
`'..'` means 'go up' → **pop** the stack, but only if it's non-empty (`..` at root is a no-op, you can't escape `/`).
Everything else is a real directory name → **push** it (names may contain dots like `...` or `a.b`, treat them literally).
Rebuild as `'/' + join(stack, '/')`; an **empty stack** yields just `'/'` (the root).
whenToUse: Canonicalize a Unix-style absolute file path
Any 'undo the last step' processing where '..' reverses a push
Resolving sequences with reversible operations (a stack mirrors history)
Token-by-token state where the most recent item is what you cancel
antiSignals: Relative paths or symbolic-link resolution against a real filesystem → needs OS calls, not pure string logic
You must preserve '.'/'..' literally (not resolve them) → it's a parsing, not a canonicalization, task
Windows-style backslash paths or drive letters → different separators and rules
You need the path's parent only → simple rsplit, no stack
remember.takeaway: A stack is the natural model whenever an operation ('..') undoes the most recent action (a pushed directory). Tokenize, fold each token into stack state, and rebuild. The same 'most-recent-cancels' shape powers expression evaluation, Backspace String Compare, and Min Stack.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you reach for a stack to model directory navigation, and whether you enumerate every token case correctly: empty, '.', '..' (with the root-boundary guard), and real names.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Forgetting that '..' at root is a no-op (popping an empty stack), mishandling empty tokens from '//', or treating multi-dot names like '...' as special when they're ordinary directory names.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Cleanly split into the four token cases up front, state the root-boundary invariant ('you can never go above /'), and rebuild the canonical path in one join — then note that names like '...' are valid directories, not navigation.

problemStatement:
You are given an **absolute** path for a Unix-style file system, which always begins with a slash `'/'`. Transform this absolute path into its **simplified canonical path**.

In a Unix-style file system, a period `'.'` refers to the current directory, a double period `'..'` refers to the directory up a level, and any multiple consecutive slashes (i.e. `'//'` or `'///'`) are treated as a single slash `'/'`. For this problem, any other format of periods such as `'...'` or `'....'` are treated as valid directory or file names.

The simplified canonical path should follow these rules:

- The path must start with a single slash `'/'`.
- Directories within the path must be separated by exactly one slash `'/'`.
- The path must not end with a slash `'/'`, unless it is the root directory.
- The path must not have any single or double periods (`'.'` and `'..'`) used to denote the current or parent directory.

Return the **simplified canonical path**.
constraints: path consists of English letters, digits, period '.', slash '/' or '_'
path is a valid absolute Unix path (begins with '/')
understanding: Take an absolute Unix path containing redundant slashes, '.' (stay put), and '..' (go up one level), and produce the shortest equivalent absolute path. We resolve navigation tokens against a directory stack, collapse repeated slashes, and never allow '..' to climb above the root '/'. Multi-dot strings like '...' are ordinary names, not navigation.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the input always an absolute path starting with '/'?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — the prompt guarantees it begins with '/'. That means the result is also absolute and I never deal with relative-path ambiguity.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How should '..' behave at the root?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: It's a no-op. You can't go above '/', so popping an empty stack does nothing — I'll guard the pop with a non-empty check.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are '...' or '..foo' special?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — only exactly '.' and '..' are navigation. Anything else, including '...' and '....', is a literal directory name to push.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should the result ever end with a trailing slash?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Never, except the root itself which is just '/'. Rebuilding as '/' + join(stack, '/') gives that for free — an empty stack yields '/'.

approaches.name: Stack of Directory Names (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The canonical answer — go straight to it. Frame it as 'split on slash, fold each token into a stack'.
hints: Walking the path, '..' has to cancel whatever directory you most recently entered. What data structure lets you undo the most recent action in O(1)?
Split the path on '/' to get components. Classify each: empty string and '.' do nothing, '..' pops, any other string is a directory to push.
Guard the pop so '..' at the root (empty stack) does nothing, then rebuild the answer as '/' joined with the stack contents.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Splitting is O(n) and each of the O(n) tokens is processed in O(1) (push/pop/skip). The final join is O(n). The stack and the output string are each at most O(n) → O(n) time and O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Canonicalizing a path is fundamentally about navigation history: entering a directory is a 'push', and `'..'` ('go up') must undo the **most recent** push. That last-in-first-out structure is exactly a **stack**, which is why the clean solution tokenizes the path and folds each token into a stack of directory names.

**Tokenizing on '/'.** Splitting the path on `'/'` turns `"/home//foo/"` into components `['', 'home', '', 'foo', '']`. Crucially, redundant slashes and the leading/trailing slash all surface as **empty strings**, which we simply skip. This is why we don't need any special pre-cleaning of `//` or trailing `/` — the split plus an empty-token skip handles them uniformly. (In Java, `split("/")` similarly yields empty entries that we filter.)

**The four token cases.** Each component is exactly one of: (1) empty string → skip (redundant slash); (2) `'.'` → skip (current directory, no movement); (3) `'..'` → pop one directory, *but only if the stack is non-empty*; (4) anything else → push it as a real directory name. The third case carries the key invariant: **you can never go above the root**. At `/`, a `'..'` has nowhere to go, so popping an empty stack must be a no-op — forgetting the non-empty guard either crashes (popping empty) or, worse in some languages, silently misbehaves.

**Why '...' is not special.** The prompt is explicit that only the exact strings `'.'` and `'..'` are navigation. A token like `'...'`, `'....'`, or `'a.b'` is an ordinary directory name and goes through the push branch untouched. Candidates who over-generalize 'dots mean navigation' get these wrong. Matching `'.'` and `'..'` by exact equality (not by 'starts with a dot') is what keeps this correct.

**Rebuilding the canonical path.** After processing, the stack holds the surviving directories in order from root to leaf. The canonical path is `'/'` followed by those names joined by single slashes: `'/' + '/'.join(stack)`. This construction gives every required property for free — it starts with a single slash, separates directories by exactly one slash, and has no trailing slash. The lone special case is an **empty stack**, where `'/'.join([])` is `''` and the result becomes just `'/'`, the root — precisely what we want for inputs like `"/../"` or `"/"`.
approaches.insight: The stack is doing one job: remembering the navigation history so '..' can reverse it in O(1). Whenever a problem has an operation that cancels the most recent prior operation, a stack is almost certainly the model. The split-then-fold structure here (tokenize, classify, mutate stack, rebuild) is a reusable template for path/expression canonicalization.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Popping an empty stack on '..'
commonMistakesDetailed.why: At the root, '..' has nowhere to go. Popping an empty stack throws in Java and silently underflows logic elsewhere. Guard the pop.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
elif part == '..':
    stack.pop()            # IndexError when at root

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Treating '...' as navigation
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Only the exact strings '.' and '..' are special. Matching by 'starts with a dot' wrongly drops valid directories like '...' or 'a.b'.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting empty tokens from redundant slashes
commonMistakesDetailed.why: split('/') turns '//' and a trailing '/' into empty strings. If you don't skip them, you push '' as a fake directory and corrupt the join.

patternNote: Stack-based token folding for path canonicalization. Recognize it when an operation undoes the most recent prior step — here '..' reverses the last directory push. Tokenize on the separator, classify each token, mutate the stack, and rebuild. The same LIFO model underlies Valid Parentheses, Backspace String Compare, and RPN evaluation.
